OF PHOTINUS THE MANICHAEAN AND PAUL THE CHRISTIAN. FIRST DISPUTATION. On the Creation of Souls. By order of the two lords Flavius Justin and Justinian, the eternal Augusti, the disputation between Photinus the Manichaean and Paul the Persian, the Christian, was held in the presence of the most glorious Theodore the prefect. It concerned the Manichaean and the Christian doctrine. The Manichaean doctrine was represented by a man who was a teacher of that religion, and the Christian doctrine by another. The disputation went more or less as follows.

MANICHAEAN. Since you and I agree that these souls are rational and intellectual, where do they get their existence? From the divine substance, since we too acknowledge that, or from somewhere else?

CHRISTIAN. Are you asking, according to the Christians' doctrine, where souls get their own existence, or something else?

M. As you wish. Tell me where souls come from.

C. I understand "from where" and "from what" in more than one sense. They can be taken as "from a substrate," as "by the maker," and in other ways. Things said in several senses must be clarified. Tell me, then: in what sense have you taken "from where" and "from" in "from the divine substance"?

M. As from a substrate.

C. In the sense of a substrate, souls are neither from the divine substance nor from anywhere else.

M. But if they are from something, are souls from God?

C. They are from the one who created them, that is, by the one who created them. For here the preposition "from" will be used rather

loosely, in place of "by."

M. So it seems you are saying that souls came into being by God from things that do not exist.

C. You have rightly understood what I have not yet said, but do acknowledge.

M. Neither common usage nor right reason has ever admitted, or ever will admit, that anything can come into being from things that do not exist.

C. Human understanding and common usage take their measure from the things around us. So let me ask you, if you will: what notion do you hold of God? That he is equal to human beings, or unequal, either by excess or by deficiency?

M. I say that God is neither equal to human beings nor inferior to them, but altogether greater.

C. Then on what grounds do you say that nothing can come into being from what does not exist?

M. From never having seen it happen.

C. Among whom?

M. Among us human beings.

C. Then how is it that, while you do not hold God to be equal to human beings, you try to show that God's works are equal to ours?

M. Where have I done that?

C. In saying that nothing can come into being from what does not exist by God's agency, just as it cannot by human agency.

M. Somehow you put your arguments forward craftily. But I know, and have received from our forefathers, and always hold fast, that nothing can come into being from things that do not exist. For if anything comes into being from things that do not exist, it will be dissolved into what does not exist; for everything that comes into being from something is dissolved back into that from which it came.

C. So it is not because nothing can come into being from what does not exist that you insist on teaching this, but out of fear that what has come into being from nonexistence may be dissolved into nonexistence. And the fear is not unreasonable. For by nature nothing at all, neither any thing nor any person, comes into being from what does not exist. Rather, it is the power of the maker that makes it, a power able to bring things forth and strong enough to grant permanence to what has come into being. So just as things were brought forth from nonexistence not by nature but by the choice of their maker, so too the permanence of things that have come into being is preserved not by nature but by the same purpose of their maker. Besides, where did you learn that everything that comes into being from what does not exist is dissolved into what does not exist, when on your view nothing has ever come into being from what does not exist, or been dissolved into it?

M. From the fact that things that come into being from a substrate are dissolved into that substrate.

C. By that argument, on your view, the same thing is both an existing substrate and a nonexisting substrate.

M. How so?

C. Nonexistent things underlie the things that come into being from nonexistents, just as what exists underlies the things that come into being from existents. Or do you put it some other way?

M. If anything comes into being from nonexistents, the nonexistents underlie what comes into being from them, just as existents underlie what comes into being from them.

C. So on your view existents are existents, and [?]. The disagreement between us, then, is not about things but about names.

M. It is a real disagreement. But since you put forward the impossible as possible, claiming that something comes into being from nonexistents, I am forced to say things contrary to my own intention.

C. If the term "nonexistents" offends you, I will not use it at all in my disputation with you. Instead I will transfer the meaning of the word in question to another word, and clearly set out my thought, which I have been expressing with the term

"nonexistents."

M. Clarify the meaning in whatever words you like.

[C.] Souls came into being by the Creator without any substrate. It was in the sense that nothing underlies them from which souls came into being that I used the term "nonexistents." So nonexistents do not underlie things that came into being from nonexistents, as existents underlie things that come from existents. Nor will such things be dissolved into nonexistents, as things from existents are dissolved into existents; for they are held together by divine power, as has been said.

M. Since you have tried to overturn by dialectic what comes from common understanding and right reason, then, as a man who deals in demonstration, show me whether souls have come into being from nonexistents, not from accepted opinions but by attending to the reality of things.

C. I will gladly do what you ask, if you answer briefly when questioned.

M. Ask whatever you like.

C. Is the method of division effective for choosing between things and distinguishing them? [?]

M. Very much so.

C. Then, using the method of division, which you and I have agreed is adequate for choosing between things and distinguishing them, I will demonstrate the proposition.

M. Keep your promise.

C. The soul, being incorporeal, rational and intellectual (this is agreed by you and me), either exists from the divine substance, or from some other substrate, or from nonexistents, or is eternal in itself. The proposition cannot be divided in any other way. Or do you put it otherwise?

M. The parts of the division are entirely true, and no other part can be added to it.

C. Well then: if it is shown that souls are neither from God, nor from some substrate, nor eternal in themselves, it follows necessarily that they came into being from nonexistents.

M. If these things are shown, then even against his will one will admit that souls are from nonexistents.

C. Do you want us first to show that souls are not from the divine substance?

M. Show that first.

C. Where is a demonstration about things drawn from? From the very existence of the things, or from somewhere else?

M. From nowhere else than their existence.

C. Do we say, then, that the attributes belonging to God and those belonging to the soul are not different from each other?

M. You speak scientifically, and that is why I am pleased with what you say.

C. Is God sinless in every respect, or does he sin in some respect?

M. God is wholly sinless.

C. And is the soul likewise, or does it sin in some way?

The Manichaean made no answer to this. After the silence the Christian said: "Even if you keep silent because you foresee the conclusion, it follows necessarily: God is sinless in every way; the soul is not sinless in every way; therefore the soul is not of the divine substance."

M. The conclusion does not follow from the premises.

C. Then prove that it is as you say.

M. I am bound in chains and cannot.

C. Even if your body is bound, your soul has not been thrown into chains. And on your view, since the body is by nature evil, the soul is rather exalted by the body's humiliation and affliction.

So you should debate all the more while in chains than without them, since through them the body is humbled and the soul is emboldened.

M. You debate with the backing of the authorities. I have no backing from any quarter, so I must keep silent.

C. Are you a teacher of the Manichaeans?

M. I am, and I confess it.

C. Do the teachers of the Manichaeans suffer for the truth, or do you put it some other way?

M. For the truth, as I reckon it.

C. Did the blessed apostle Paul have the backing of the authorities when he was in chains? Or did he neglect his own teaching while in chains because he lacked it?

Here too the Manichaean kept silent and gave no answer.

C. If you keep silent because you are unwilling to debate, you yourself do not know why. All the same, I will not leave out the rest of my demonstrations; for I have not yet set out all the arguments showing that souls are not from the substance of God.

M. Say whatever you like. I am glad to follow what is said, provided I am not forced to debate; for a certain illness has come upon me.

[C.] The divine substance is indivisible, but according to you souls are parts of the divine substance. So either the indivisible substance will be divided, which is absurd, or souls are not of the divine substance.

M. Just as flakes come from gold and rays from the sun, so souls come from God.

C. Somehow you debate without being forced, now pleading illness, now entering the debate like Momus. Nevertheless, I will now examine what you have said. Do the flakes come from the gold by cutting and division, or not?

M. They are parts of the gold.

C. Do you say the same of God?

M. The same.

C. Then how is the divine substance indivisible, when it has been divided into many parts, as gold is into flakes?

M. As regards its substance the divine substance is indivisible, but as regards the dispensation it is divisible.

C. Then for what reason was the divine substance divided, when it is indivisible?

The Manichaean kept silent and said nothing. After the silence the Christian said: "Even though you are silent, I will tell those present the solemn doctrines of your dispensation, by which God, though indivisible, was divided."

M. It is up to you whether to speak or not.

C. Among the Manichaeans there is one principle that is good and another that is evil, and both are eternal. But at a certain time a kind of madness and war arose between these principles, not by the choice of both, but by the principle of evil. For according to them that principle, having seen the light of the good, wished to seize it and to shake his kingdom. The good God, seeing the aggressor, and seeing that if he did not stir himself but kept to himself he would be plotted against by his adversary, formed within himself the following plan: to put forth certain parts of his own substance and throw them to the opposing principle. And this he did. The evil principle, having received the divine portions, as the Manichaeans call them (whether they wish to call them parts, or [?], or sections, or something else), went down into its own abyss, holding the divine sections within itself. This, then, according to my opponent and the Manichaeans, is the

dispensation, and the premise of the dispensation, through which God, though indivisible, was divided. [?] This premise, which does not even need refuting, has been overturned [?], the dispensation of the Manichaeans. And if the dispensation has been overturned, the divine substance remains indivisible forever, though the Manichaean hypothesis had forced it and carried it off into division. I refute it as follows. The good God, or the divine substance, feared the evil either as being stronger than the evil, or as equal to it, or as weaker. If as stronger, the claim is absurd; for being stronger himself, he would not have feared what is weak. If as equal, the evil will be equal to the good in power; but they do not say this. If he feared it as weaker, that is still more absurd; for they make the evil stronger than the good, which these men themselves concede. Since by this division their doctrine has been shown to be absurd, both the dispensation and its cause are gone; and the divine substance, being indivisible, was not divided for the sake of a dispensation that does not exist. Besides, if God is indivisible as regards his substance, then souls are not from God as regards his substance, as the Manichaeans claim. But enough of that.

I can also say other things on the subject, and they are these. If the divine substance [?] lives in a mortal and corruptible body as one that needs it, then the soul is not from the divine substance. Further, the soul will at some time forget what it knows, but God will never forget what he knows; therefore the soul is not from the divine substance. Further, God in no way needs the senses, that is, sight, hearing, smell and taste, to carry out his own activities, but souls do need them; therefore souls are not of the divine substance.

M. The soul was formerly reason, and was hearing, and was sight, and was taste, and was touch. But now, having been cast into the body, it has become capable of hearing from hearing, rational from reason, capable of touch from touch, [?] capable of smell from smell.

C. In the first place, as has been shown, the soul was not formerly reason, or hearing, or sight, or smell, [?] this has been received. Next, is God himself reason, from whom the soul comes, so that the soul too, being from God, is reason? Or do you put it some other way?

M. God is reason, and hearing, and the rest; [?] and the soul, before it was cast into the body, was such as God is.

C. [Every?] reason is the reason of something, and every hearing is the hearing of something. And if God is hearing and reason, God will be found to be something else's

reason; which [?]

Here too the Manichaean kept silent and gave no answer. After the silence the Christian said: "Since the course of the argument has passed over the second example, that of the rays and the sun, this too must be examined. The rays coexist with the disk, and the disk is the cause of the rays. But souls do not always coexist with God; rather, on account of the dispensation,

and according to my opponent himself, they came into being at a certain time. Therefore souls do not come from God as rays come from the sun. Further, the rays, though they come from the disk, are in no way dissolved into the substance of the disk. But souls, according to my opponent, will one day be dissolved into the very God from whom they came. Therefore souls do not come from God as rays come from the sun.

By these arguments I have shown that souls are not of the divine substance. That they are not from any substrate either is plain. For if the soul is incorporeal and rational, and nothing incorporeal or rational comes into being from a substrate, it is clear that the soul does not either. Nor indeed is it eternal in itself, for it is under a debt to the body [?], both in glorifying and in giving thanks. If it had not come into being by God, it would owe him nothing; but it does owe him, so it came into being by him. For the soul does not owe God the offering of glory and thanksgiving in the way you hold, but as one that came into being by him. If, then, it is neither from the divine substance, nor from some substrate, nor eternal in itself, it is clear that it came into being from nonexistents, that is, without any substrate, by God as its creator.

The End, with God.

SECOND DISPUTATION. On the Two Principles of the Manichaeans. Following on the second [?] disputation, after one day had passed, in accordance with the arrangement agreed by each side, the following was debated.

MANICHAEAN. Today I will be the one asking questions, since in the previous disputation our positions were put to the test.

CHRISTIAN. Your positions were put to the test in the previous disputation, as you say, but not all of them. All of them ought to have received the proper examination, and only then should you have begun on ours. But since you would like to test ours before yours have been properly examined, ask whatever you like.

M. What are the subjects you wish to lead us to?

C. Is your question that of one who is learning or of one who is debating?

M. For the present I have chosen not to debate but to learn.

C. Then you have granted me the role of teacher?

M. I have granted it to you.

C. Among us Christians, along with other things, there is a main doctrine of this kind, which we hold and teach: that some things are in our power. Since you choose to learn, you must accept this first of all. And if you also wish to learn the demonstration of it, I will try to give it. After this main doctrine and its demonstration, I will gladly tell you, if you wish, the remaining main doctrines of our teaching, with their proper demonstrations.

M. You have begun your teaching from the middle of things, not from the beginning.

C. Whose part is it to say what starting point of teaching suits the learner: the learner's, the teacher's, or someone else's?

M. The teacher's.

C. Then it is for me to begin the teaching wherever I wish.

M. Since you said that some things are in our power, tell me first: who are we?

C. What you have said is the part of one who is debating, not of one who is learning.

M. I am not learning; I am

debating now.

C. Then put your question again.

M. Who are we?

C. We are human beings by nature.

M. That is not what I want to learn, but whether we are composite or simple.

C. The first question did not include this. Since the second does, I say that on our view we are composite, but on yours we are not.

M. How is it that on our view human beings are not composite?

C. What is a human being composed of? Of like parts or of unlike parts?

M. Of unlike parts.

C. Are they all perceptible, or are some intelligible as well?

M. Some are intelligible as well.

C. On your view the intelligible parts, being sections of the divine substance, in no way enter into composition with their opposites. For opposites enter into composition with opposites through intermediates, or an intermediate; but on your view there is nothing intermediate between good and evil. So on your view the good will not enter into composition with the evil.

M. I do not know how you can say that on the view of us Manichaeans human beings are not composite. But answer me this: are human beings composite on your view?

C. On our view human beings are composite.

M. Of what is a human being composed?

C. First, of body and soul. Second, souls are composed of their own parts, if one must speak of parts in the case of souls. And the body consists of the four elements.

M. Is the substance of bodies most generic, or not?

C. Of which bodies?

M. Of all of them.

C. In terms of the universal, the substance of bodies is most generic.

M. [?] And that of souls?

C. Again, which souls do you mean?

M. Human souls, of course.

C. In terms of the universal, it too is most generic.

M. If, then, the substance of bodies is most generic, and the intelligible substance of souls is also most generic, it necessarily follows that there are two principles without beginning.

C. The conclusion you have drawn does not follow from the premises you have set out.

M. How so?

C. Is the substance of plants most generic in terms of plants, or not?

M. Most generic.

[C.] And is that of the elements also most generic in terms of elements?

M. That too is most generic.

C. If, then, there are two principles because the substance of bodies is most generic and that of souls is another, then because the substance of plants is also most generic and that of the elements is another, you must speak of more than two principles here too. Besides, if [?] substance, as substance, does not differ from substance, but is itself the substance of all things [?], then one principle is established from its being most generic.

M. [It is] itself; as substance, every substance is included.

C. Is substance most generic when it is taken in terms of bodies and souls, or when it is considered insofar as it is substance?

M. When it is taken in terms of substance, substance is most generic.

C. If, then, there are two principles because the substance of bodies and that of souls are most generic, then, since substance is more truly most generic in its own terms, there is only one principle.

M. Explain more plainly whether anything is in our power. C. Among us Christians, the things that exist are divided roughly as follows: some of them are in our power, while others depend on the nature of things. Of the things in our power, we ourselves are the makers and causes; of those that depend on nature,

[?] And what do you mean by the things that depend on the nature of things? C. What is in our power are the evils and goods defined by law, for which a recompense has been laid down: evils such as impiety and sin, and goods such as piety and virtue. M. Where do evils come from? C. From the will. M. Where does the will come from? C. From the soul. M. Where does the soul come from? C. According to you, from the divine substance, and so according to you evils too come from the divine substance. According to me, though, the soul comes from nothing, and so evils too come from nothing. M. You have no argument against what is said according to our doctrine. But I will try to show that even according to us evils do not come from the divine substance. Evils come from the soul when it is compelled, not when it chooses. C. Where does the soul come from? M. From the divine substance. C. Do you people agree that the soul carries the divine substance within itself, or not? M. It carries it. C. Is there anything stronger than the divine, able to compel the divine substance? At this the Manichaean fell silent too and gave no answer. The Christian spoke again: Are you willing to accept that something is in our power? M. Not at all. The things thought to be in our power exist by participation in substances that existed before them. The heat in us does not exist of itself but by participation in the heat that is in fire, and the cold in us does not exist of itself but by participation in the substance of water. In the same way the evils in us exist by participation in the good [?] principle. C. Does our body partake of [?] by nature, and of water by nature, or do you put it some other way? M. By nature. C. And are the things that belong to nature of necessity forbidden or commanded by law? M. I don't know what you mean. C. Since you have taken what is clear to be unclear, let us clarify the matter with examples. The heat in us is not commanded of our nature by law, for it occurs by nature, of necessity. The same is true of [?], conversely: not by legislation but by nature. But the evil in us, that is, [?] or fornication or something of that kind, and the good, that is, piety and virtue, are a different matter: under the law the former are forbidden and the latter commanded. If, then, we have these things by participation, as we have heat and cold, the law is superfluous, both the [?] law and the divine. Besides, no punishment or reward has been laid down for natural things and things that happen of necessity. Yet for things of the kind said to be in our power, both punishment and reward have been declared. So these things do not happen by nature, as heat and cold do. If not by nature, then by choice; and if they are by choice, then the point at issue, that something is in our power, has been proved. M. Even if you have cunningly established that something is in our power, the evils that exist in the nature of things

you will never refute or escape. C. What evils do you take to exist in the nature of things? M. When animals die, their bodies decay, and before the decay they give off such a stench that it drives away friends and enemies alike. I leave aside the fact that even before the stench, which is the prelude to dissolution, foul-smelling sores arise in our bodies. And then dung and urine have the same kind of smell. C. Of these evils too, if they really are evils as you say, the soul is the cause. M. How so? C. Stone and wood are bodies, and according to you earth and wood belong to evil matter. According to you people there is less soul in these, and yet they do not stink, nor are they thought to by any [?]. But in the bodies of animals, which the stench accompanies, there is more soul according to you. Now the soul is the cause of the binding together of bodies, and dissolution follows the binding together of bodies, for if there had been no composition there would be no dissolution. Since the soul is the cause of composition, and dissolution follows composition, the soul is also the cause of dissolution. But if the stench is the prelude to dissolution, then the soul is also the cause of the stench. And if the alteration of food happens neither in stones nor in wood, but in the bodies of animals, then clearly the alteration of food in animals happens through the power of the soul. If so, the soul is also the cause of the stench of dung, and in the same way of sores. At this the Manichaean was thrown into utter confusion and said nothing.

THIRD DISCUSSION. On the Divine Scriptures of Both Testaments. Three days later a discussion took place. When they met on the third day, the following questions were raised. MANICHAEAN. Since both you and I praise and expound the divine Scriptures, why do you [?] the things written in divine Scripture that support our doctrines? CHRISTIAN. What is there in the teaching of Scripture that you think supports your doctrines? M. Does Paul say that flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, or not? C. I know that he says it. That it supports your doctrines I do not know. M. According to Paul, whose doctrine is it to place the flesh, and indeed all visible things, outside the kingdom, if not ours, the Manichaeans'? C. It is ours rather than yours to place the flesh outside the kingdom. M. Then why do you also disparage the flesh and estrange it from God's creation? C. It seems that I call one thing flesh and you another. So tell me what you define flesh to be. M. The flesh that we and the other animals wear. C. Neither the Apostle nor I called that flesh. M. How is it clear that the Apostle did not call this flesh, but something else? C. From the Apostle himself. M. Where does the Apostle say this? C. In what he adds:

"nor does corruption inherit incorruption." M. That does not make it clear that the Apostle did not call this flesh, but some other, as you claim. C. It is clear, and if you like I will put it more plainly. M. Make it as plain as you wish. C. Is the pairing of flesh and corruption an equal one, and is it set in contrast with [?]? M. I don't know what you mean. C. Is a contrast ever drawn between things that have no substance of their own and things that have substance, and does this happen in Paul? M. I don't know whether it has. C. Suppose, then, that Paul does not draw his contrast between what has substance and what has none. Here corruption is set against flesh, and by your own account corruption has no substance of its own, so flesh has none either. How then, by your account, did the Apostle give the name of flesh to this flesh? Or do you also say that corruption is without substance in the same way as flesh? M. The logic constrains me, but what was said is a puzzle both for me and for you. C. For you it is a puzzle, but not for me. If I show that Paul was not speaking of the flesh you named, but that here too he means something without substance of its own, as in the case of corruption, then for me the puzzle is solved, while for you it remains forever. M. Go through the argument in detail. C. Divine Scripture calls none of the incorruptible and immortal things flesh. Sometimes it even excludes mortal and corruptible things from this designation, as when it says: "But you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit." This does not mean that they are not now in flesh, but that they do not set their minds on things that deserve corruption and dissolution. M. So it seems that, on your account, the Apostle called the dissolution of the flesh "flesh." C. It was my part to establish this and yours to listen. But since you have anticipated me and stated the idea, the truth is no different. M. And what would you say about "The flesh lusts against the spirit," and the reverse? C. The same idea applies: he called the dissolubility [?] and corruptibility of the flesh "flesh." Until our body comes to be free of this and of corruption, it is called flesh, but once it is released from this, it also lays aside the name of flesh. So both statements are true: that flesh and blood do not inherit the kingdom of God, and that the soul's choice, which the Apostle called spirit, is one thing, while the things our mortality seeks, which the Apostle called flesh, are another. M. Isn't this the Apostle's: "Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from the body of this death?" C. It is the Apostle's, and it holds to the same ideas. Here the Apostle speaks not of doing away with the body, but of doing away with the body's death. M. What about this: "I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive to the law of sin which is in my members"? C. Since you like examining such passages of Scripture, tell me: does the Apostle here disparage the members of the body, or the law of the members? M. He speaks of a law, a law of sin, which is in our members. And since this law, being the law of the members, is disparaged, necessarily

the things the law belongs to are disparaged along with it. C. That argument wipes out all the doctrines of the Manichaeans. M. In what way? C. According to Manichaean doctrine, is there sin dwelling by necessity and force in the soul, which is good and comes from the divine substance? M. There is such sin. C. And is such sin disparaged? M. It is disparaged. C. Then how is the soul that has the sin disparaged along with the sin? M. I don't know how you have cunningly escaped this argument as well. C. What do you say about the Old Testament, seeing that Christ by his deeds and the Apostle by his words disparaged the Old Testament everywhere? M. I cannot set out everything that tells against the Old Testament all at once, since the discussion proceeds by question and answer. But if you wish, I will put it forward piece by piece. C. Tell me piece by piece the things in the Old Testament that you think are disparaged. M. Is "The law works wrath" the Apostle's, or not? C. It is the apostle Paul's, and it contains great praise of the Old Testament. M. If that contains praise, then nothing in life could be found that contains blame. C. That is laying down a law, not debating. In debate the proper course is to ask how it contains praise, not to counter with a verdict. M. Tell me, then, how this contains praise of the Old Testament. C. The Old Testament distinguished good from evil, and clearly took both as matters of choice. It attended to people's right actions and failures. It praised those who did right and judged them worthy of rewards, but it punished those who failed and brought wrath upon them. Since, through their own wickedness, people sinned more than they did right, the law was seen to inflict the punishment of wrath. In that sense the law works wrath. M. It seems that you take "The law came in so that the trespass might increase" in the same sense [?] too. C. Naturally. Because its truth surpasses everything, the word of truth brings even those who want to flee from it onto the same road. M. Did Christ keep the Jewish Sabbaths in his actions, or did he abolish them? C. He both kept them and abolished them. He kept them in their season, and abolished them as the season of the [?] Testament advanced. M. When was it the season of the Old Testament, and when was it not? [?] C. Until his baptism Christ was living in the season of the Old Testament, and he did everything the Old required, fulfilling the law of Moses on our behalf. After his baptism he began the [?] of grace and offered people the teachings of the New. So with Christ we find neither an abolition of the observances of the law before his baptism, nor an observance of them after it. At this the Manichaean fell silent again and gave no answer. The next day the Manichaean's depositions before the prefect were read to the Christian. He found that in them

the God of the Old Testament was slandered as wicked, so the Christian questioned the Manichaean again: Is the God of the Old Testament one God and the God of the New another, or are they one and the same? M. They are two different Gods. The one is good and the other bad; the one is good and the other wicked. C. Do you accept what is written in the New Testament as spoken by the good God, or do you put it some other way? M. I accept it. C. Then if, according to you, the God of the Old Testament is one God and the God of the New another, and Moses is the author of the Old Testament, how could Jesus say in the New Testament: "Moses wrote about me, and if you believed his writings, you would also believe my words"? And how could Paul write in the Epistle to the Romans: "Since God is one, who will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith"? M. Who is the maker of darkness? C. According to the Manichaeans, the good God. M. How so? C. Who made heaven and earth? Wasn't it the good God? M. That is what I say. C. And isn't darkness contained within these? M. It is contained within them. C. Then how could the one who made the things that contain it not also have made what they contain? M. There is another darkness besides the visible one, which lies outside heaven and earth, and this visible darkness is part [?] of that one. C. Where did our discussion start from: from what is plain to everyone in common, or from Manichaean supposition? M. From the common understanding, obviously. C. Then does the common understanding know of another darkness outside heaven and earth, of which the darkness we see is a part, or does this belong to Manichaean opinion? M. Whatever agrees with common usage and right reason, and whatever deserves to be taught, and the solutions to passages in divine Scripture that seem to support our doctrines: all this I have examined carefully, learned and received. But I cannot give up my long-held, old prejudice and conceit. C. My part was to establish the truth and refute the falsehood. It is not my part to overturn people's will as well, for a human being is free to choose.
